newsitem.title: INDIA: India budget can be passed even after trust vote.
newsitem.headline: India budget can be passed even after trust vote.

text.p: India's budget for 1997/98 can be passed even if the embattled government fails to win a vital vote of confidence next week, the speaker of the lower house of parliament said on Wednesday.

Hong Kong-based STAR TV later quoted unnamed sources in the Congress party, on whose support the budget's passage is heavily dependent, as saying the party planned to steer the budget for the fiscal year starting April safely through parliament.

"The proposal is still to come but I assure you that the Congress will not do anything which will create a financial or economic crisis," senior Congress member Pranab Mukherjee told STAR's mainly Indian news programme.

The market-friendly budget presented on February 28 was called into question on Sunday after the Congress party withdrew its make-or-break support for Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front coalition.
"There is a precedent that even after the resignation of the government, the budget has been taken up," speaker P.A. Sangma told reporters at Parliament House.

On Tuesday, coalition leaders said they were exploring the possibility of trying to push the budget that would slash corporate and personal tax rates through parliament before the trust vote set for April 11.
Sangma said it was up to government to decide when the budget would be put to a vote in parliament. "I do not foresee any crisis on the budget," he added.
Parliamentary Affairs Minister Srikanta Jena earlier told Reuters that Sangma was under pressure to ensure that the budget was not held hostage to the political crisis.
Asked if the government had begun meeting political parties to make sure the budget was passed, Jena said: "There is nothing so far. The whole thing is in the Congress camp."
Attempts to salvage the budget ran into a snag on Tuesday when the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) said a budgetary vote could not be considered before the confidence vote.
For the budget to be passed, the minority government would have to work out an agreement with either the Congress Party or the BJP.
BJP vice-president K.R. Malkani said a vote on the budget could not precede the confidence vote because spending proposals needed first to be discussed by parliamentary panels.
Parliament had earlier been scheduled to take up the budget after reconvening on April 21.
The BJP controls 193 deputies in the 545-seat Lok Sabha, the lower house of parliament. The Congress has the support of 140 and Deve Gowda's coalition commands 180 lawmakers.
